To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the transfer function of warm dark matter is characterized by two scales, the free streaming scale k{sub fs} and the horizon crossing scale k{sub hor}, and that the transfer function has a plateau in the range k{sub fs}/k{sub hor} approx. 0.5-2.5.
warm dark matter power spectra have a plateau at small scales and that the amplitude of the plateau depends on the particle mass and the shape of its distribution function.

the transfer function of warm dark matter is characterized by a plateau at small scales, which is a direct consequence of the early integrated Sachs-Wolle effect, and that the power spectrum of sterile neutrino dark matter candidates is suppressed on small scales, but not enough to alleviate the small scale problems of standard cold dark matter models.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the power spectrum of warm dark matter is not as smooth as previously thought, and that the acoustic oscillations of the baryon fluid leave a clear imprint on the power spectrum of dark matter.
the power spectra of sterile neutrinos in the keV mass range are not significantly affected by the early integrated Sachs-Wole effect.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we provide a semianalaytic derivation of the evolution equations, their solutions and a simple numerical code to obtain power spectra and transfer functions for arbitrary distribution functions.
warm dark matter models can have a rich phenomenology at small scales that can be understood analytically.
warm dark matter models with m{approx}<keV are not ruled out by current data.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, at small scales, the power spectrum for warm dark matter candidates is a simple function of the mass and the velocity dispersion at decoupling, and that the power spectrum for a given mass is a function of the velocity dispersion at a given redshift.

the power spectra of sterile neutrinos are significantly suppressed at small scales, with the amount of suppression depending on the mass of the sterile neutrino and the strength of the coupling to the standard neutrinos.
warm dark matter models with m{approx}<keV are viable, with power spectra that are not suppressed at small scales, as long as the distribution function is nonthermal.
